messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Its me Paul Hughes just signing off.  I have finished my project and have 
found S very useful.  I started of with no knowledge about S or statistics 
in general, I now know nothing and a bit.  I would like to express my 
gratitude to all the people that have been kind enough to help.  In 
particular I would like to thank Prof Ripley and Jose Pinheiro who have 
helped me several times throughout my time with you.  I will end by telling 
you what I did because it might interest some of you and also because you 
may be able to shed some light on my findings.

I performed a simulation study to try to quantify the effects of staggared 
recruitment on the estimation of treatment effect using Laird-Ware 
regression at 6,12,24 and 48 month interim monitoring times.  I have 
suggested a method of quantifying the effect of recruitment on estimation of 
the treatment effect.  I had hoped by including the recruitment into a 
laird-ware model the estimation of the treatment effect would stabilize 
around the true value quicker than if recruitment was not considered.  This 
was not the case, I had found when I compared two models, one with 
recruitment, internal time and treatment and the other just internal time 
and treatment, the estimation of the treatment effects where the same.  I 
specified the simplest random effects structure, a random intecept.

Can anyone suggest why this is so, and when it might not be so?  With the 
ultimate aim of more efficiently modelling biological phenomena  can anyone 
envisage a situation where including recruitment might lead to a quicker 
estimation of the treatment effect.  Any suggestions would be helpful.

Anyway thats what I did, very badly.  I am really sad to go and never 
thought I could have feelings for people that I wouldn't know from adam.  
Take care love to you and yours, see you on the other side!

Paul.

messages.subject: Summary: Probability Illustration
messages.body_plain:
My request was for a method to  plot a normal density curve, a vertical 
line, and then shade the area underneath the tail to the right of the 
line.  I planned to use dnorm() for the curve, but I didn't know how to 
draw the shading.

I thank all who applied.  In order of arrival time, they were Kevin Brand, 
Tim Hesterbert, Andy Liaw, Peter Alspach, Don MacQueen, Jim Stapleton, Joe 
Davis, and Tom Jagger.

The most-recommended method was using polygon(), but the *simplest* method 
was due to Jim Stapleton.  His method draws vertical lines to shade the 
tail, as in his example:

> x <- seq(-4,4,.01)
> plot(x,dnorm(x),type="l")
> lines(c(-4,4),c(0,0))
> g <- function(x0){z <- seq(x0,4,.01)
+ for(xz in z)lines(c(xz,xz),c(0,dnorm(xz)))}
> g(2)

I adopted that method, which should also reproduce well for publication.

If anyone would like copies of the other examples, please email 
me.  Otherwise I won't take the time and space to broadcast them.

Thanks again!

--
Michael Prager, Ph.D.                <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>

messages.subject: CODE Summary: Probability Illustration
messages.body_plain:
The request was for a way to plot a normal density curve, a vertical line, 
and then shade the area underneath the tail to the right of the line.  I 
received many helpful responses, posted a short summary, and have received 
many requests for more detail.  Thus, this compilation of the suggestions 
that included S-Plus code. My apologies if I've overlooked anyone or failed 
to give credit where due.

Again, thanks to all for responding!  Much appreciated.

MHP

=============================================================
Kevin Brand <Kevin_Brand at hc-sc.gc.ca> wrote:

I had slapped something together (see below) to make this plot a while 
back.  Its probably not the most efficient way, but hopefully it provides 
at least a  start.

----------S-code to illustrate prob of false positive (one sided) ------
x_seq(-3,5,length=400)
plot(x,dnorm(x,0,0.5),type="l",xlab="X",ylab="Probability
Density",ylim=c(0,1.5))
#lines(x,dnorm(x,1.0,0.5),col=3)
tmp_qnorm(0.95,0,0.5)
tmpy_dnorm(tmp,0,0.5)
segments(x1=tmp,x2=tmp,y1=0,y2=tmpy,lwd=4,col=3)
segments(x1=tmp,y1=0,x2=max(x),y2=0,lwd=4,col=3)
tmpp_tmp
tmpn_qnorm(0.975,0,0.5)
dtmp_(tmpn-tmpp)/4
for(i in 1:15){
tmp_tmp+dtmp
tmpy_dnorm(tmp,0,0.5)
segments(x1=tmp,x2=tmp,y1=0,y2=tmpy,lwd=4,col=3)
}
rm(tmpn,tmpp)
abline(v=c(0),lty=2)

=============================================================

Don MacQueen <macq at llnl.gov> suggested using polygon() (as did numerous 
other responses) and also mentioned the plot option to draw vertical lines 
from the horizontal axis to the point.  Don also pointed out:  "I believe 
that a number of people have written code shading tails, so you might find 
something at statlib, or in the snews archives."

=============================================================
Jim Stapleton gave the following simple approach (which I used successfully):

x <- seq(-4,4,.01)
plot(x,dnorm(x),type="l")
lines(c(-4,4),c(0,0))
g <- function(x0){z <- seq(x0,4,.01)
  + for(xz in z)lines(c(xz,xz),c(0,dnorm(xz)))}
g(2)

=============================================================

...to which Bill Dunlap <bill at insightful.com> added the following 
refinement (also suggested by Mrigesh Kshatriya <mkshatriya at parks-sa.co.za>):

If the vertical lines work well enough (the number of lines to draw depends 
a bit on the graphics device you use), then you can do it faster using

g2 <- function(x0)
{
z <- seq(x0, 4, 0.01)
lines(z, dnorm(z), type = "h")
}

type="h" means to draw vertical lines between the y values given and y=0.

You can use it with plot() or lines() (or points(), which is the same as 
lines(type="p")).

=============================================================
Tom Jagger x367 <tjagger at insightful.com> sent this approach using polygon():

Just, thought I'd play around with the plot.polygon function, and came up 
with the following starting material:

plot.tail <-
function(z, zmax = 3, side = "right", space = 0.01, ...)
{
x <- seq( - zmax, zmax, space)
y <- dnorm(x)
plot(x, y, pch = ".")
sign <- c(-1, 1)[match(side, c("left", "right"))]
if(is.na(sign))
stop("side is one of left or right")
index <- which(sign * x >= sign * z)
if(sign < 0)
index <- rev(index)
ys <- y[index]
xs <- x[index]
polygon(c(z, xs, sign * zmax), c(0, ys, 0), ...)
}

#try:
plot.tail(2)
plot.tail(-1)
plot.tail(-1,side="left",col=2)

# etc.

# the ... is for passing additional arguments to S.

# You can add additional overlays and use different graphics patterns as 
needed.

=============================================================
Scott Chasalow <scott.chasalow at cereon.com> set the following set of functions:

"shade.norm"<-
function(mean = 0, sd = 1, weight = 1, lower.prob = 0.95, upper.prob =
0.999,
plot = T, plotfun = "matlines", type = "h", lty = 1:5, col = 1:6, ...)
{
# DATE WRITTEN: 14 May 1999 LAST REVISED: 14 May 1999
# AUTHOR: Scott Chasalow (Scott.Chasalow at cereon.com)
#
# DESCRIPTION:
# Shade a specified area under the curve of one or more normal
densities.
#
# SEE ALSO:
# draw.norm, draw.normmix
#
# EXAMPLES:
#
# draw.norm()
# shade.norm(lower=0.95)
#
# draw.norm()
# shade.norm(lower=0.001, upper=0.025)
# shade.norm(lower=0.975, upper=0.999)
#
# draw.norm(0:1)
# shade.norm(0:1, lower=0.001, upper=0.025)
# shade.norm(0:1, lower=0.975, upper=0.999)
#
n <- max(length(mean), length(sd))
mean <- rep(mean, length = n)
sd <- rep(sd, length = n)
weight <- rep(weight, length = n)
x <- NULL
y <- NULL
for(i in seq(along = mean)) {
x <- cbind(x, as.matrix(qnorm(seq(lower.prob, upper.prob, length =
10000), mean[i], sd[i])))
y <- cbind(y, as.matrix(dnorm(x[, i], mean[i], sd[i])))
}
y <- y %*% diag(weight)
if(plot) {
eval(parse(text = plotfun))(x, y, type = type, lty = lty, col =
col,
...)
invisible(return(NULL))
}
return(list(xmat = x, ymat = y))
}
"draw.norm"<-
function(mean = 0, sd = 1, weight = 1, plot = T, tit = T, plotfun =
"matplot",
type = "l", lty = 1:5, col = 1:6, xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)", ...)
{
# Date written: ? Last revised: 6 May 1993
n <- max(length(mean), length(sd))
mean <- rep(mean, length = n)
sd <- rep(sd, length = n)
weight <- rep(weight, length = n)
x <- NULL
y <- NULL
for(i in seq(along = mean)) {
x <- cbind(x, as.matrix(qnorm(seq(0.001, 0.999, length = 1000),
mean[
i], sd[i])))
y <- cbind(y, as.matrix(dnorm(x[, i], mean[i], sd[i])))
}
y <- y %*% diag(weight)
if(plot) {
eval(parse(text = plotfun))(x, y, type = type, xlab = xlab, ylab =
ylab, lty = lty, col = col, ...)
if(tit)
title(paste("Normal density:\nmean =", deparse(mean), ", sd
=",
deparse(sd)))
invisible(return(NULL))
}
return(list(xmat = x, ymat = y))
}
"draw.normmix"<-
function(mean = 0, sd = 1, weight = 1/n, plot.it = T, tit = T, plotfun =
"matplot", type = "l", xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)", lty = 1:5, col = 1:6,
...)
{
# DATE WRITTEN: 16 April 1993 LAST REVISED: 14 February 1996
# PURPOSE: Plot a mixture of normal distributions
#
n <- max(length(mean), length(sd))
if(length(weight) > n)
warning(
"Length of argument 'weight' greater than
max(length(mean),length(sd)); extra values in argument 'weight' were
ignored"
)
mean <- rep(mean, length = n)
sd <- rep(sd, length = n)
weight <- rep(weight, length = n)
x <- NULL
y <- NULL
for(i in seq(along = mean)) {
x <- cbind(x, as.matrix(qnorm(seq(0.001, 0.999, length = 1000),
mean[
i], sd[i])))
}
xx <- sort(unique(as.vector(x)))
for(i in seq(along = mean)) {
y <- cbind(y, as.matrix(dnorm(xx, mean[i], sd[i])))
}
weight <- as.matrix(weight)
yy <- y %*% weight
if(plot.it) {
eval(parse(text = plotfun))(xx, yy, type = type, xlab = xlab, ylab
=
ylab, lty = lty, col = col, ...)
if(tit) {
wtstring <- paste("c(", paste(as.character(weight),
c(rep(",",
n - 1), ""), sep = "", collapse = " "), ")")
mtext("Normal-Mixture Density:", line = 2, cex = 1.5)
mtext(paste("means =", deparse(mean), ", sds =", deparse(sd),
", wts=", wtstring), line = 1, cex = 0.75)
}
invisible(return(NULL))
}
return(list(x = xx, y = as.vector(yy)))
}
======================================================

--
Michael Prager, Ph.D.                <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Center for Coastal Fisheries and Habitat Research
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516
http://shrimp.ccfhrb.noaa.gov/~mprager/

messages.subject: Summary and Exhortation: Greek in Axis Labels
messages.subject_clean: Summary and Exhortation: Greek in Axis Labels
messages.body_plain:
I mentioned needing Greek in axis labels (xlab, ylab), and I received three 
suggestions:  (1) use R, (2) use a control character, (3) use psfrag with 
LaTeX.  I believe all are potential solutions, and I thank those who 
suggested them.  I will probably persue psfrag, although it involves far 
too much fiddling for my own taste.

I am perplexed at why we can't get rudimentary math (Greek, subscript, 
superscript, italic, and bold) added to S-Plus traditional 
graphics!  Plenty of folks ask about it, and there is no shortage of Rube 
Goldberg solutions, but when I talk to Insightful about this issue, I feel 
I'm the only one who's ever requested it.

I exhort all paying S-Plus customers who would like to have this facility: 
please contact Insightful and put your name on an enhancement request!

If S-News readers think I have gone over the edge on this issue, please 
drop me a private note to let me know.  I'd apreciate that.

If anyone from Insightful is reading this, would you please let us users 
know how we can influence you to add this feature?

MHP

--
Michael Prager, Ph.D.                <Mike.Prager at noaa.gov>
NOAA Center for Coastal Fisheries and Habitat Research
Beaufort, North Carolina  28516

> I am trying to analyse the proportion of seeds that

> =binomial , weights= sown, data = sensvu)
>
> this seems to work fine, but

(I would use glm(cbind(germinated, sown-germinated) ~ treatment,
family=binomial, data=sensvu) as it initializes better.)

> anova(sv.glm, test="Chisq")
>
> churns out highly significant results when graphs
> suggest little difference. Have I done this correctly?

If those really were the results, then I get

Terms added sequentially (first to last)
          Df   Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev  Pr(Chi)
     NULL                       3   21.62707
treatment  1 0.07261131         2   21.55446 0.787572

which is of course not `highly sigificant'.  So we need to know more.

But one issue here is that under treatment B you have unexplainable
differences between the two results, and hence a lot of over-dispersion.
(One experiment gives 90% success, another 50%.  Extermely implausible when
each is out of 50.  Try fisher.test.) Given this, the model is not
plausible and hence the Chisq test that assumes binomial variation
is not believable.

messages.subject: Further question on loess()
messages.body_plain:
S-Plus users
E-mail: s-news at wubios.wustl.edu

Hi!
   Dr. Alec Stephenson's comment made me modify my object,
and the object leads to the satisfactory result. The modified object is:

##
        span1 <- 0.5
        x0 <- 2.3       #  
##
        nd <- 20
        set.seed(110)
        xx <- seq(from = 1, length = nd, by = 0.1)
        xx <- xx^3
        yy <- cos(xx * 0.8) + rnorm(nd, mean = 0, sd = 0.3)     ##
##
        assign("data1", data.frame(x1 = xx, y1 = yy), frame = 1)
        fit.lo <- loess(y1 ~ x1, data = data1, span = span1, family = 
"gaussian", degree = 1, 
                surface = "direct")     ##
##
        data2 <- data.frame(x1 = x0)    ##
        ey2 <- predict.loess(fit.lo, newdata = data2)   ##
##      
        print("LOESS in S-Plus")
        print(ey2)      ##
##
##
        kk <- as.integer(span1 * length(xx))
        dis <- ifelse(span1 < 1, sort(abs(xx - x0))[kk], span1 * sort(abs(xx - 
x0))
         [length(xx)])
        wt <- rep(0, length(xx))
        yes1 <- abs(xx - x0) <= dis
        wt[yes1] <- (1 - (abs(xx[yes1] - x0)/dis)^3)^3
        coef1 <- lsfit(xx, yy, wt)$coef
        ey3 <- coef1[1] + x0 * coef1[2] ##
##
        print("My LOESS")
        print(ey3)

   It seems that "data1" for loess() must be placed in "frame 1" when "surface 
= "direct"
is designated.

The result is:

[1] "LOESS in S-Plus"
[1] -0.1819646
[1] "My LOESS"
  Intercept 
 -0.1819646

It looks nice.
   My further question is why "surface = "direct"" is undesirable.
The manual on "loess.control()" says:

surface determines whether the fitted surface is computed directly at all 
points ("direct") or
whether an interpolation method is used ("interpolate"). The latter, the 
default, is what most
users should use unless special circumstances warrant.

I suppose that many LOESS users would like to obtain estimates by LOESS based
on its definition described on standard textbooks on nonparametric regression.
I wonder whether I should not recommend use of "surface = "direct"" for
novice users of loess().

> |> family=binomial, data=sensvu) as it initializes better.)
> 
> This subject is mentioned on page 219 of V&R3 but I didn't find any
> explanation as to why that form "...allows the fitting function to
> select a better starting value..."

(It's called: read the code ....  Not sure why you would expect a detailed 
tecnical explanation there.)

It's a bug in binomial()$initialize.  From 6.0:

expression({
        if(is.matrix(y)) {
                if(dim(y)[2] > 2)
                        stop("only binomial response matrices (2 columns)")
                n <- drop(y %*% c(1, 1))
                y <- y[, 1]
        }
        else {
                if(is.category(y))
                        y <- y != levels(y)[1]
                else y <- as.vector(y)
                n <- rep(1, length(y))
        }
        w <- w * n
        n[n == 0] <- 1
        y <- y/n
        mu <- y + (0.5 - y)/n
}
)

As n is one in the weighted form, the last line gives starting values of
0.5 whatever the data.  However, as the glm fitting problem is log-concave,
it should only affect the number of iterations needed.  However, the
convegence criterion in glm is notoriously lax and given the Hauck-Donner
effect there can occasionally be premature stopping from 0.5.

I think the final line should be something like

        mu <- (n * y + 0.5)/(n + 1)
 

> I am interested in this topic because I am dealing with some BEFORE
> and AFTER data.  The AFTER values are usually smaller than the BEFORE
> values but not always, so I couldn't use a difference.  In
> desperation, I tried using the AFTER as success and BEFORE as failure.
> The glm didn't object and the inferences made from the analysis of
> deviances seemed to make sense.
> 
> Was I just lucky, or is there a sensible explanation?

One could see this as a 2-group test of counts, if independence held.
Given k pairs of values what glm would fit is a 2 x k contingency table
test of (some null hypothesis about the model).

messages.subject: Replacing Lower Triangular Elements
messages.body_plain:
My thanks to Peter Ellis, Steve McKinney (Insightful), Elizabeth
McKinnon, Andy Liaw, Bill Dunlap (Insightful), Charla Lambert
(Insightful), David M. Smith (Insightful), Rolf Turner, Gerald
Jean.  Your responses were quite helpful.

The most common response was to use :

my.matrix[lower.tri(my.matrix) & my.matrix==2] <- 3

As Rolf Turner pointed out my confusion lay with the fact that
lower.tri returns a vector, not a matrix.

Steve McKinney provided further comment:
>Pulling the lower triangular portion of the matrix
>yields an ambiguous structure.  Since S-PLUS does
>not have a lower triangular matrix object programmed
>into the matrix accessor functions, the lower triangular
>portion of the data is returned as a list (in a particular
>order so that you can write code to index the values
>in proper order

Charla Lambert pointed out that I could reference elements in the
lower triangle as follows:
U[row(U) > col(U)] <- 0

David Smith picked up a subtle point.  In my initial attempt, I had
written
(my.matrix [lower.tri(my.matrix)] ) == 2
David says
> isn't the comparison you wanted to make.  (Sordid details: 2 is
coerced to
> T, so this relation is a no-op.)

Thank you everyone!

Alastair Dempster

messages.subject: Mixed Effects Models
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Users,

I am having trouble specifying a mixed-effects model using LME.  The data
set consists of several blind concentrations submitted to a group of
laboratories on a given date. Each lab produces 1 result for each blind
sample.  The entire procedure is repeated over 12 dates.

The desired model is of the form:

Response = Lab + Date + Concentration + LabxDate + LabxConcentration,

where Lab is a fixed effect, and date, concentration and their interactions
are random effects.  Lab, date and concentration are blocking variables
(factors in Splus or class variables in SAS).  While easy enough to run
using Proc Mixed, I am having trouble with specifying the model in Splus.
Any help would be appreciated.

Sincerely,
Barry Zajdlik.

messages.subject: Adding equations to a mutlipanel plot
messages.subject_clean: Adding equations to a mutlipanel plot
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Thanks to Marcel Baumgartner, Matt Kurbat, Dave Atkins, and Jim Pratt for their
ideas on how to superpose two lines on a multipanel plot.

The following seems to do the trick:

xyplot(formula,
   data = data,
   groups= sample,
   aspect=1,
   subset=(sample== t1)|(sample== t2),
   xlab ="log(dose)",
   ylab ="response",

   panel= function(x,y,subscripts,groups){
   groups <- as.numeric(as.factor(groups))[subscripts]
   max.groups <- max(groups)
   N <- seq(along = groups)

     for(i in sort(unique(groups))) {
        which <- N[groups == i]
        j <- which
        points(x[j],y[j],col=1,pch=i)
        abline(lm(y[j]~x[j]),col=i)
     }
   })

I have another question. How do I insert regression equations onto each of the
   panels?

Thanks,
Frustrated student

messages.subject: Create folders in Command window
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

 

Many thanks to: Peter Alspach, Samantha Low 
Choy, Greg Snow, Jingshan Zhang for replying to my message. Below are my 
question and the answers I have collected.....

 

Question:

 

I run Splus 2000 on Win98, and I am 
working in the Command window. How can I 
create folders where I can put my files of different projects? And how 
can I manage these folders ( for example, cut-copy-paste, 
files).

I have created a lot of objects and datasets and 
when I type :

 

> objects()

 

Answers ( the order of the answers is like the name's order 
above)

You could check out Mark Bravington's utilities for project management in 

SPlus: http://www.cefas.co.uk/splus/splus.htm.

Also, 
given that object.summary() gives the creation time (I think the format 
of 
the creation time may be platform and version dependent), it is possible to 

write a function to list only objects created before, or after, a certain 
time.  
Below follows a somewhat crude version that I have written for 
SPlus 2000 
on Windows 95:

dnew <- function(After=T, Days=0, 
Last='omit')
{
#  Assumes objects.summary() gives creation time in 
number of seconds 
since
#  noon on 1 January 1970
  td <- 
date()
  td <- paste(substring(td,9,10), substring(td,5,7), 
substring(td,21,24), sep='-')
  td <- as.numeric(dates(td, 
format='day-mon-year', origin=c(1,1,1970)))
  td <- 
24*60*60*(td-0.5-Days)
  o.list <- cbind(obj=objects(), 
secs=objects.summary()[[5]])
  o.list <- 
o.list[order(o.list[,2]),]
  if (Last=='omit') o.list <- 
o.list[substring(o.list[,1], 1, 5)!='last.' 
&
                                     
substring(o.list[,1], 1, 6)!='.Last.',]
  if (After) 
as.factor(o.list[as.numeric(o.list[,2])>=td,1])
  else 
as.factor(o.list[as.numeric(o.list[,2])<=td,1])
}

 

Hi Thodoris, 
I suggest learning about the workspace feature in S-plus : its main purpose 
is to help organize data from different S-plus projects. You will still have to 
organize your other files relevant to stats projects (eg Word documents, Excel 
raw data, etc) using the File Explorer... 
If you find the workspace feature weird, there is also a nice shortcut method 
of isolating your S-plus projects. 
Create a shortcut to the S-plus program 
icon (found as sp2000/cmd/splus.exe), then right-click on the short-cut and 
choose Properties, and on the Shortcut tab, and in the Target box, add some text 
setting the project path, eg add 
    S_PROJ = 
"n:\sama\project1\phase1\stats" 
Let me know if you have any difficulty... 
Sama 

You can create a new folder/database/directory using the 
new.database
function

When you have multiple databases, use attach to 
gain access to one, and
detach when you are finished.  By default attach 
will put a new database
into position 2 which means that you can use the data 
in it, but anything
new that you create will go into whichever database is in 
position 1 (use
search() to see the current positions).  To add new data 
to a database,
attach it at position 1, then all new data created will go 
there.

hope this helps,

Try Insert folder in the main menu 
after
switching to the objects window, then
drag all the needed files into 
it.

jingshan

messages.subject: testing for ANOVA
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-newsers,

I have a straightforward ANOVA question.

Consider a 2-way ANOVA model, such as

fit.2way <- lm(y ~ treatment + nnrti, data=actg)

Running the anova() command I get:
fv>  anova(fit.2way)
Analysis of Variance Table
Terms added sequentially (first to last)
           Df Sum of Sq  Mean Sq  F Value      Pr(F) 
treatment   3    6.6470  2.21566  2.37301 0.06971484
nnrti       1   50.1968 50.19681 53.76172 0.00000000
Residuals 435  406.1555  0.93369                    

Question:  What is the interpretation of the "treatment" test?

For the longest time I thought that this is exactly the test
for the "treatment" factor from the 1-way ANOVA model (i.e., ignoring the 
second factor, "nnrti"), but it is not:

fv>  fit.1way ~ lm(y ~ nnrti, data=actg)
fv>  anova(fit.1way)
Analysis of Variance Table
Terms added sequentially (first to last)
           Df Sum of Sq  Mean Sq  F Value      Pr(F) 
treatment   3    6.6470 2.215661 2.116848 0.09738108
Residuals 436  456.3523 1.046680                    

(The 1-way ANOVA and 2-way ANOVA yield same treatment SS, but the F-tests
have different residual SS and Df).

Also, in general this is not the same as the "standard" test for the
"treatment" factor, after controlling for "nnrti", unless the design
is balanced.

Thanks for the insights,

        Florin

============================
Florin Vaida
Assist Prof, Dept of Biostatistics
Harvard School of Public Health 
655 Huntington Ave Boston MA 02115
Tel (617) 432-2914

Limited seats available for two courses presented by Dr. Frank Harrell, Jr in 
Washington DC! Register now!

Course #1

S-PLUS for Statistical Data Analysis and Graphics ~

S-PLUS for Statistical Data Analysis Course Summary: This three-day course 
begins with a quick summary of the S-PLUS language and objects and a comparison 
of S-PLUS and SAS. This is followed by methods for inspecting, re-coding, 
re-shaping, and manipulating data, some of which use extensions of S-PLUS found 
in the public domain Hmisc library written by the instructor. Usage of S-PLUS 
for more advanced statistical methods such as simulation and bootstrapping is 
surveyed. Then basic sample size and power calculations are discussed, followed 
by an example using the Hmisc library to simulate power for the Cox-logrank 
test for comparing event times in a clinical trial in which drop-in, drop-out, 
and delayed treatment response are present. Then major emphasis is given to 
table making and S-PLUS and Hmisc graphical functions useful in everyday 
exploratory work and to present final summary statistics. The course concludes 
with discussion of some tools for making analyses reproducible,!
 an important facet for regulatory and other scientific review of final 
results. Advantages of using S-PLUS in conjunction with the LATEX document 
processing / typesetting system for constructing reproducible statistical 
reports and hyperlinked PDF documents are discussed. The course will utilize 
both lecture and interactive laboratory format. 

Prerequisites for this course: Knowledge of a statistical package or a 
programming language and experience in statistical data analysis. A good 
understanding of S-PLUS basics is assumed. This is not the course to learn 
S-PLUS basics.

Regression Modeling Strategies ~ 
http://www.insightful.com/train/harrell_regression.html  

Date/City:      June 4 - 6, 2001 Washington, DC

Course Summary: The first part of the course presents the following elements of 
multivariable predictive modeling for a single response variable: using 
regression splines to relax linearity assumptions, perils of variable selection 
and overfitting, where to spend degrees of freedom, shrinkage, imputation of 
missing data, data reduction, and interaction surfaces. Then a default overall 
modeling strategy will be described. This is followed by methods for 
graphically understanding models (e.g., using nomograms) and using re-sampling 
to estimate a model's likely performance on new data. Then the public domain 
S-PLUS Design library will be overviewed. Design facilitates most of the steps 
of the modeling process. Next, statistical methods related to binary and 
ordinal logistic and survival models will be covered. Four case studies will be 
presented: an interactive exploration of the survival status of Titanic 
passengers, a case study in data reduction and modeling of an ordinal clin!
ical diagnostic outcome, an interactive case study in developing a survival 
time model for critically ill patients, and a case study in Cox regression. In 
the hands-on computer lab, students will develop, validate, and graphically 
describe multivariable regression models themselves.

Prerequisites for this course: A good general knowledge of statistical 
estimation and inference methods and a good command of ordinary linear 
regression. Those who want to run the laboratory exercises themselves or who 
want to use S-PLUS to use the methods taught in this course in their everyday 
work should have had a previous introduction to S-PLUS. Participants are 
encouraged to read references available on the following website:

messages.subject_clean: Summary and Exhortation: Greek in Axis Labels
messages.body_plain:
Mike Prager wrote:
> I mentioned needing Greek in axis labels (xlab, ylab), and I received three
> suggestions:  (1) use R, (2) use a control character,
>
> (3) use psfrag with LaTeX.  I believe all are potential solutions, and I
> thank those who suggested them.  I will probably persue psfrag, although it
> involves far too much fiddling for my own taste.
Here's a work around I hacked together (in windows) to (give the
appearance of) writing a string with multiple fonts.

ttext<-function(x,y,string,font=NULL,height=NULL) {
 if (is.null(height)) height<-rep(0,length=nchar(string))
 if (is.null(font)) font    <-rep(1,length=nchar(string))
 for (i in 1:nchar(string)) {
    par(font=font[i])
    a<-par()$cxy[1]
    b<-par()$cxy[2]
    text(x+a*i,y+.5*b*height[i],substring(string,first=i,last=i))
}
}

#And some examples

plot(0,0,xlim=c(1,10),ylim=c(1,3),axes=F,xlab="",ylab="")

par(cex=1.5)

ttext(1,2,"Blah! Proportional 
Fonts",font=c(1,8,3,8,4,8,5,8,6,8,7,8,1,8,3,8,4,8,5,8,6,8,7,8))

a<-"A quick brown fox jumps"

b<- "over the lazy dog"

ttext(1,3,a,font=sample(1:10,size=nchar(a),replace=T))

ttext(1,2.5,b,font=sample(1:10,size=nchar(b),replace=T))

ttext(1,1,"The ith circle has formula Area = 
pr2",font=c(rep(1,34),8,rep(1,10)),height=c(0,0,0,0,0,1,1,rep(0,29),1,1,1,1))

ttext(1,1.25,"The ith circle has formula Area = 
pr2",font=c(rep(3,34),8,rep(3,10)),height=c(0,0,0,0,0,1,1,rep(0,29),1,1,1,1))

par(cex=1)

The three main drawbacks are
1) it's probably device dependent - you have to know the font numbers
for your device.
2) it doesn't handle proportional fonts properly
3) it's fiddly having to write the font and height numbers in.

Fix-ups -
2) can be handled by have a character/spacing table for each font!!
3) shouldn't be to difficult to overcome, you could have something
like  string = "The <h=1>i<h=0>th quick brown fox<f=2>fads<f=1>"
and parse the string within the ttext function to create the "height"
and "font" vectors.

[This solution maybe similar to Mike's 2 but I'm not sure what it
does. ]

Megan Pledger

messages.subject: Re: testing for ANOVA
messages.body_plain:
I also laboured under this impression for a while.
Then like you I noticed that I got different F-tests
depending on the rest of the model.  I then did lots
of different anova tables, like this:
 anova(lm(y ~ nnrti + treatment, data=actg))
 anova(lm(y ~ treatment + nnrti, data=actg))
 anova(lm(y ~ treatment, data=actg))
 anova(lm(y ~ nnrti, data=actg))
 
In an MSc practical I did Sir David Cox pointed out to me
that this is not the conventional/right approach.  (Note this 
is my memory from 6 years ago so I hope I am not misquoting 
him - all errors in this are certainly my own!).  

The only difference between the two tests you have done is in 
the residual sum of squares (ie the error variance).  If nnrti is 
a candidate explanatory variable then you should estimate the residual 
sum of squares after fitting it (in general you should estimate 
this residual error variance from the largest sensible possible
model) - ie you should only look at the first two anovas above.  
This is particularly obvious in your example as nnrti explains 
a lot of variance and so changes the RSS a lot.  

In your case I suspect it does make most sense for you to do only 
one anova: 
   anova(lm(y ~ nnrti + treatment, data=actg))
since treatment is (presumably) the effect you are most 
interested in.  It is better then to consider its significance 
_after_ fitting for the nnrti effect.  As you say the F value 
will then be different for treatment unless treatment and nnrti 
are orthogonal.

>Question:  What is the interpretation of the "treatment" test?
What I think you are essentially asking is the difference between
the F values for treatment in the two anovas from:
  (i) y ~ nnrti + treatment
 (ii) y ~ treatment + nnrti
My way of understanding this is that when nnrti and treatment 
aren't orthogonal then there is some SS which is explained by
_either_ of them.  If you want to attribute this explanatory 
power to nnrti then use (i) above; if to treatment use (ii) 
above.  This is why the 'philisophical' light in which you view 
the variables does matter, and why I suggest that (i) is probably
the right choice for your example.

This is my current level of understanding - but I would be 
interested to hear if people disagree !

Cheers,  Andrew

>I have a straightforward ANOVA question.

>Consider a 2-way ANOVA model, such as

messages.subject: dll.load with Fortran
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-PLUS Gurus,

I'm trying to test out whether my Fortran compiler can produce DLL's that are
compatible with my version of SPLUS (SPLUS-2000 for Windows).  I'm trying the
dll.load approach, but am experiencing problems.

The Fortran compiler is MS-Powerstation and it states in the manual that "the
only platform box possible for this compiler is Win32" which sounds to me like a
hint of incompatibility, but I've charged ahead just to make sure.  Does anyone
know if this caveat does indeed spell out incompatibility (my knowledge of DLLs
is near nill).   In case it could be possible, my Fortran code and Splus calling
function are shown below (the function is the one  presented as an example in
the Splus Programmer Guide (p. 563) --- albeit translated from C++ code, in
which it originally appeared.

FORTRAN CODE-----

SUBROUTINE arsim(x,ndim,phi)
!MS$ATTRIBUTES DLLEXPORT :: arsim
INTEGER ndim
REAL x(ndim), phi

IF( ndim .gt. 1)THEN
     DO 10 i=2,ndim
          x(i) = phi*x(i-1)+x(i)
10   CONTINUE
ENDIF
RETURN
END

------

SPLUS calling function

r.compiled_function(x=1:20,phi=0.75,ndim=length(x)){
dll.load("C:\\MSDEV\\Projects\\testlink\\Debug\\testlink.dll", symbols="arsim")
storage.mode(x)    <- "single"
storage.mode(ndim) <- "integer"
storage.mode(phi)  <- "single"
res_.Fortran("arsim",x,ndim,phi, NAOK=0, specialsok=F)$x
return(res)
}

----

Calling this routine yields the following error statement

> Error in .Fortran("arsim",: "ARSIM" is not a symbol in the load table

Any suggestions on what might be missing, or perhaps example code of success
stories would be greatly appreciated (the SPLUS
manual examples are mostly in for C++).   Also any insight about my prospects
given the possibly dated Fortran compiler
would also be appreciated!!

thanks in advance,

Kevin

messages.subject: Summary: predict.gam(newdata = ) with bs() model
messages.body_plain:
Many 
thanks to all who responded including (I hope I get everyone) Anne York, Greg 
Snow, Nick Ellis, and Thomas Yee.

 

My 
problem was in building a spline basis with bs(), then feeding that into lm. The 
resulting lm object could not be fed into predict() or predict.gam(). Apparently 
this was discussed on this list in December; I apologize for missing 
it.

 

The 
easiest solution is to put the bs() call into the lm() call.

 

Nick 
Ellis pointed this out to me. When the result of bs() is kept 
separately, lm() has no idea that that thing is a spline basis and predict() 
doesn't know it's supposed to do anything special. (In retrospect this is 
obvious. Sorry.) Thomas Yee said the same thing Nick did. He was 
perhaps too  modest to point out his web site 
(with T. Hastie) at http://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/PEOPLE/yee/smartpred/index.shtml 
, which discusses exactly this problem in some detail. 
Anne York was nice enough to bring that 
web site to my attention. Greg Booth also sent a nice reply that included the 
observation that in this case predict.gam() could not figure out the "type." 
When it was supplied explicitly, that part of the problem went 
away.

 

Many 
thanks to all.

 

Sam 
Buttrey

buttrey at nps.navy.mil

messages.subject_clean: Summary : How can I draw X-Y plot with multiple Y axes?
messages.body_plain:
I want to thank everyone who took the time to help solve the
following problem I sent out on 24 May:

Question: 

How can I draw X-Y plot with multiple Y axes? 

10|       Line A _/              /    |100
 9|            _/          _____/     | 90
 8|          _/           /           | 80
 7|        _/            /            | 70
 6|      _/             /             | 60
 5|    _/         _____/ Line B       | 50
 4|  _/          /                    | 40
 3| /           /                     | 30
 2|/           /                      | 20
 1|                                   | 10
 0|                                   |  0
 -----------------------------------------

Line A and B are plotted based on left Y axis 
and right Y axis, respectively.

Here is a summary of above question.

Jason Connor's advice:

# Here is an example that either came from S-Plus help or from Cleveland's
examples:

sun.agg <- aggregate(sunspots, 1, "mean")
par(mar=rep(5, 4))
tsplot(rain.nyc2, ylab="rain in inches")
legend(1946, 65, c("rain", "sunspots"), lty=1:2)
par(new=T) # trick to add plot with different scale
tsplot(window(sun.agg, start(rain.nyc2), end(rain.nyc2)), axes=F, lty=2,
lwd=2)
axis(4)
mtext("mean number of sunspots", side=4, line=3)
title(main="New York Rainfall and Sunspot Activity")

Tom Richards's advice:

Use plot() with axes=F option,
then use the axis statements, with
axis(side=2)
and
axis(side=4)

Nick Locantore's advice:

One way to do this is to plot the data for line A, using:
plot(..., yaxt='n')
        This 'turns off' the y-axis marks.  Then, you would need to scale
the data for line B to match line A's boundaries.  In your example, you
would plot line B's values divided by 10.  Then plot this using lines.
        Then, use the axis() function to create the y-axis bounds. For your
example, it would be something like:
axis(2, at=0:10, labels=0:10)
axis(4, at=0:10, labels=seq(0,100,10))
        2 denotes the left y-axis, and 4 denotes the right y-axis in the
axis function.

Anne E. York's advice:

"Twoplots" <- 
function(x1, y1, x2, y2, type = "l", xlim = NULL, ptitle = "Twoplots", xlab
= "x", ylab1 = "y1", ylab2 = "y2", ...)
{
# Written by AE York Sept. 1996
# Plots y1 vs x1 and y2 vs x2 on the same plot
# Labels for y1 are on the left and labels for y2 on the right
        oldpar <- par()
        par(mar = rep(6, 4))    #       
        if(missing(xlim))
                xlim <- range(pretty(range(c(x1, x2))))
        plot(x1, y1, lty = 1, pch = 1, type = type, xlim = xlim, xlab =
        xlab, ylab = ylab1, ...)
        par(new = T)
        plot(x2, y2, lty = 2, pch = 16, type = type, axes = F, xlim = xlim,
        xlab = "", ylab = "")
        axis(side = 4)
        mtext(ylab2, side = 4, line = 2, outer = F)
        par(oldpar)
        title(ptitle)
}

Tim Hesterberg's advice:

Use axis(..., side=3) to add the axis on the right.
You may want to ensure there is room by using par(mar=...)
before creating the plot.

Dr. Greg Snow's advice
# scaling the second line

plot( xa, ya, xlim=range(xa,xb), type="l")
lines( xb, yb/10, lty=3)
tmp <- pretty( yb/10 )
axis(4, at=tmp, labels = tmp*10,srt=90)

# overlaying 2 plots

old.par <- par()
plot( xa, ya, xlim=range(xa,xb), type="l")
par(xaxs="d", new=T) # force next plot to use same x axis and don't clear
screen
plot( xb, yb, type="l", axes=F, lty=3, xlab="", ylab="")
axis(4)

Jim Pratt's advice:

1) standardize the YA and YB to run from 0-1.
2) par(5,4,4,5)+.1  #add space to right side for axis labels and title
3) plot(x,YA,yaxt='n',type='l',col=1,lty=1,xlab='X title',ylab='YA
title')
4) lines(x,YB,col=2,lty=2)
5) axis(side=2,at=seq(0,1,by=.1),labels=0:10)
6) axis(side=4,at=seq(0,1,by=.1),labels=seq(0,100,by=10))
7) mtext(side=4,'YB title',line=3)

Renaud Lancelot's advice:

> x <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length = 100)
> y <- cos(x)
> z <- 10 + sin(x)
> par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 4))
> plot(x, y, type = "n", axes = F)
> lines(x, y, col = 2)
> axis(1)
> axis(2)
> par(new = T)
> plot(x, z, type = "n", axes = F, col = 3, xlab = "",
        ylab = "")
> lines(x, z, col = 8)
> axis(4)
> mtext(side = 4, text = "z", line = 2.5)
> box()

On Sat, 26 May 2001, Michael Ian Westphal wrote:

>     Does anyone know how to fix the values of the intercept and coefficients

That's what offset() is for.  Compute the linear predictor lp at your fixed
values and use

fit <- glm(y ~ offset(lp) - 1)

Unfortunately, it seems to have slipped thorugh various cracks in the

messages.subject: Summary: operating on the name of a dataframe
messages.subject_clean: Summary: operating on the name of a dataframe
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to everyone who replied to my query. My first reply (from Andrew
Sinclair below) was back in just 20 minutes. There was a lot of overlap in
the replies so only a selection is given below.

Thanks again,
Glenn

Original query>
>Does anyone know how I can operate on the name of a data frame 
>passed as an
>argument to a function? I want to write code that does the 
>following but can
>not find a way to make it work. Any suggestion would be 
>greatly appreciated.
>
>f(df)
>{
> if ((name of dataframe)=="UK")
>   { ... }
> else if ((name of dataframe=="USA")
>   { ... }
}> 
>

From:   ASinclair at maninvestmentproducts.com
[mailto:ASinclair at maninvestmentproducts.com]
<mailto:[mailto:ASinclair at maninvestmentproducts.com]>
Sent:   24 May 2001 10:15
To:     Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com
Subject:        RE: [S] Operating on the name of a dataframe

Two ways to proceed:
### define test data frames
UK  <- data.frame(x=1:10,y=rnorm(10))
USA <- data.frame(x=1:10,y=rnorm(10))

(1)     Pass in the name of the data frame as a string:

myfun1 <- function(dataframename){
                dataframe <- get(dataframename,where=1)
                if (dataframename=="UK"){ 
cat('UK data:\n') print(dataframe)
         }
else if (dataframename=="USA"){            
cat('US data:\n') print(dataframe)
         }
return()
}
myfun1('UK')  ### pass string
myfun1('USA') 

(2)     Probably better, using  deparse(substitute())

myfun2 <- function(dataframe){
                dataframename <- deparse(substitute(dataframe))
                if (dataframename=="UK"){ 
cat('UK data:\n') print(dataframe)
         }
else if (dataframename=="USA"){            
cat('US data:\n') print(dataframe) 
         }
return()
}
myfun2(UK)  ### pass dataframe
myfun2(USA) 

Hope this is what you wanted,
Andrew

From:   Nick Locantore [mailto:nick at Waratah.com]
<mailto:[mailto:nick at Waratah.com]> 
Sent:   24 May 2001 12:40
To:     'Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com'
Subject:        RE: [S] Operating on the name of a dataframe

Glenn,
If I recall correctly, the argument to the function will be character text,
so you would call f(df="USA").  When passed, you can use the if statement
you have.  For the (...) part, you will need to start with the following:
work.df <- eval(parse(textß))
This will have the effect of making work.df the data.frame USA or UK inside
the function.  Once assigned, just perform calculations as normal, except
use work.df.
Hope this helps,
Nick Locantore
Waratah Corporation
www.waratah.com <http://www.waratah.com> 

-----Original Message-----
From:   Rolf Turner [mailto:rolf at math.unb.ca]
<mailto:[mailto:rolf at math.unb.ca]> 
Sent:   24 May 2001 13:35
To:     Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com <mailto:Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com> 
Subject:        Re: [S] Operating on the name of a dataframe

The required incantation to get a hold of the name of ***any***
argument to a fuction ("dataframe" is irrelevant) is
deparse(substitute())
as in
f(df)
{
ndf <- deparse(substitute(df))
if (ndf=="UK")
   { ... }
else if (ndf=="USA")
   { ... }
}

cheers,

Rolf Turner
From:   David L Lorenz [mailto:lorenz at usgs.gov]
<mailto:[mailto:lorenz at usgs.gov]> 
Sent:   24 May 2001 15:21
To:     Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com <mailto:Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com> 
Subject:        Re: [S] Operating on the name of a dataframe

Glenn,
The argument passed to the function is the actual data and there is no name
associated with that object.  Therefore, you must generate a name for it
from the call.  Here's some code that you might try.
f <- function(df) {
df.name <- as.character(match.call()$df)
if(df.name == "UK") ...
}
Dave

From:   Nick Ellis [mailto:nick.ellis at marine.csiro.au]
<mailto:[mailto:nick.ellis at marine.csiro.au]> 
Sent:   25 May 2001 00:40
To:     Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com <mailto:Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com> 
Subject:        RE: [S] Operating on the name of a dataframe

Getting the name of the argument is usually done with deparse(substitute())
> fun <- function(x) {deparse(substitute(x))}
> fun(x)
[1] "x"
> fun(x*10)
[1] "x * 10"
> fun(qqwd)  # argument needn't exist: try random name
[1] "qqwd"
> exists("qqwd")
[1] F
It is not necessarily a good idea to create code dependent on the name of
the object. It's unlikely to work if your function is embedded deep within a
stack of function calls. An alternative would be to give the data frame an
attribute, "state", say, and test using that. E.g.
> f(df)
> {
>  if (attr(df,"state")=="UK")
>    { ... }
>  else if (attr(df,"state")=="USA")
>    { ... }
>
> }

with calling code
mydf <- <define the data frame>
attr(mydf,"state") <- "USA"
f(mydf)

Nick Ellis
CSIRO Marine Research   mailto:Nick.Ellis at marine.csiro.au
<mailto:Nick.Ellis at marine.csiro.au>

<mailto:[mailto:dmurphy at cc.umanitoba.ca]> 
Sent:   24 May 2001 23:12
To:     Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com <mailto:Glenn.Treacy at ilim.com> 
Subject:        Re: [S] Operating on the name of a dataframe

This was discussed a day or two ago in R-news. I think the trick here is to
make df a names object. Here's a toy function that I think gets what you're
after:
> mtest <- function(x) {
*       dfr <- as.name(x)
*       if(dfr=="UK") cat(paste(dfr, "is in Europe\n",sep=" "))
*       else if(dfr=="USA") cat(paste(dfr, "is in North America\n",sep=" "))
*       else cat(paste(dfr, "is somewhere on Planet Earth\n"))
+  }
> mtest("UK")
UK is in Europe
> mtest("USA")
USA is in North America
> mtest("Chile")
Chile is somewhere on Planet Earth
Of course, you can replace the cat() statements above with any (block of)
code you desire.
Hoping this is of some help,
Dennis

Glenn,
You probable just need something like...
dfname_deparse(substitute(df))

The reverse can be useful at times...
df_eval(parse(textßname))

messages.subject: S-PLUS v. SAS: Cox models with time dependent covariates
messages.subject_clean: S-PLUS v. SAS: Cox models with time dependent covariates
messages.body_plain:
Dear All

Should I be surprised to get different results under S-PLUS (version 3.4,
Unix) compared with SAS (version 6.12) when running a Cox model with a time
dependent covariate?

Taking the famous Stanford heart transplant data, fitting the model :
   coxph(Surv(start, stop, event) ~ transplant + age, data=heart,
method="breslow")
yields estimated regression coefficients of -0.00275 for transplant and
0.03074 for age (where age refers to age at entry, and not age at
transplantation).
In the SAS manual for PROC PHREG, the same model yields coefficients of
-0.06046 for transplant and 0.03147 for age.
i.e. S-PLUS gives an estimated hazard ratio for transplant of 0.997
(exp(-0.00275)), whereas in SAS it's 0.941.

I wondered whether there were some errors/differences between the dataset
used in the SAS manual and that contained in the data frame "heart" in
S-PLUS.  However, reading "heart" into SAS, modifying to force one line only
per patient, the same model gives a coefficient of -0.06776 for transplant
(hazard ratio=0.934) i.e. similar(ish) to that given in the SAS manual.

I would be very grateful if someone could explain why I cannot reproduce
this result in S-PLUS.

Thank you very much,

Nigel Yateman

messages.subject: Re: Efroymson's method
messages.body_plain:
Hi Winfred,

Maybe this will get you started.......?  Once you get this then
maybe your other questions will become more clear.
"I'd like to know what a partial correlation is"

Well, a partial correlation is the correlation between the unique part
of the dependent variable (Y) correlated with the unique part of some other
variable (X1), controlling for the other variables in the model. 
That is, a partial correlation between Y and X1 is the correlation between
the parts of Y and X1 that cannot be explained by other variables in the
model.  It helps to think of this of this as the correlation of the
residuals from Y being predicted from the the other independent variables
(Excluding X1) with the residuals from predicting X1 from the other predictors.

 (This is different from the Part of Semi Partial Correlation
that correlates all of Y with the unique part of some X variable....Note
that the partial correlates only part of Y and Part of X-those parts that
are independent).
I'm not at all familiar with the Specifics of the Efroymson Method.

Ken

The issue here is that the other version is a 64-bit version of S. If it
had been a 32-bit version, any post 4.0 version of S-PLUS would read
the objects.  (They automatically cope with big-endian vs little-endian,
and AFAIK all such platforms use the same IEEE formats for reals.)

The only really safe way I know is to find some kind soul with S-PLUS on a
Dec Alpha to run data.dump on your objects, and data.restore the dumps on
Solaris.

messages.subject: Couple of questions on trellis xyplot
messages.subject_clean: Couple of questions on trellis xyplot
messages.body_plain:
I'm using trellis graphics to plot some data. The call
xyplot(SKR ~ YEAR | BASETMTF, data = Skr1, as.table = TRUE)
produces a dot plot of the variable SKR as a function of
YEAR, with a separate panel for each value of BASETMTF. 
After reading the manuals, and the online help, and looking
at the menu options, I can't figure out hot to do a couple
of the things that I'd like to do.

1) The panel strip label across the top of each panel is black,
and hides the text label for that panel. How do I make it white,
so that my labels show through?

2) The dots that represent the data points are open. How do I 
make them solid black?

3) I'd like to plot a loess line in each panel. There's an example
of how to do this on p. 280 of the Programmer's Guide. When I try
to apply that example to my situation, I get an error message that
says something like "Argument y not matched: ", and then a string
of numbers that are the values of YEAR, each replicated four times.
Presumably, there's something I need to do first, or something I 
need to add to the function call as given in the manual to get it 
to work. Does anybody know what that might be?

regards,
Mark A.
